strengths: Strong empirical results: ~5× speedup on large models (GPT2 7B) with <0.2% loss difference, substantially outperforming prior progressive training work (2-4×)

Novel insights on 'mixing behaviors': Useful observation that progressive and fixed-size training converge similarly when comparing entire training trajectory, providing new understanding of when/why progressive training succeeds
Well-motivated theoretical framework: Proper use of muP for initialization design and hyperparameter transfer, enabling consistent LR across model size changes without retuning
Comprehensive empirical validation: Experiments across GPT2, ResNet, and MoE with hundreds of runs and detailed ablations on optimizer states, schedules, batch sizes, and architectural variations
Sound convergence analysis: Section 4 provides theoretical intuition framing progressive training as 'PGD + initialization + SGD', even if not directly applicable to non-convex settings
Thorough experimental documentation: Extensive hyperparameter specifications, multiple configurations tested, and detailed appendices supporting reproducibility
Clear presentation: Well-organized writing with effective 'takeaway' boxes and figures that clearly illustrate key findings
weaknesses: Significant theory-practice gap: Convergence analysis assumes convex and G-Lipschitz loss, but deep learning is non-convex. While citing similarity results, the bounds apply to running averages, not final iterates, with unclear practical implications

Critical dependence on specific experimental setup: Results heavily rely on Muon-NSGD optimizer with muP scaling and WSD schedule; generalization to other optimizers/schedules unclear. Figure 5 shows WSD schedule is crucial but this may limit applicability

Limited baseline comparisons: Primarily compares against fixed-size and progressive training variants. Missing comparisons to knowledge distillation, width scaling, or other recent efficient training methods (e.g., comprehensive comparison with Du et al. 2024, Pan et al. 2024)

Incomplete speedup attribution: 80% compute savings partly stems from training shallow models longer. Not clearly isolated how much improvement comes from progressive training efficiency versus simply using smaller models. Section C.1 provides partial evidence
Lacks statistical rigor: No error bars, confidence intervals, or significance testing despite claiming <0.5% loss differences. Unclear if small loss gaps are within statistical noise
Architectural generalization concerns: ResNet shows different behavior with random initialization (Appendix A.3), suggesting method may not generalize uniformly across architectures

Theoretical simplifications limit applicability: Assumes large model as [w_t, x_t] concatenation despite layers being inserted; muP analysis incomplete for non-residual paths; mixing time defined informally without precise quantification

Limited scope of evaluation: Largest model tested is 7B; single primary dataset (OpenWebText); no analysis of interaction with distributed training or gradient accumulation; unclear if results scale to 10B+
Code and reproducibility concerns: No mention of code release; strong dependence on Muon optimizer may limit adoption; some architectural choices (n_head values) appear arbitrary
Incomplete failure analysis: Limited discussion of when method fails, architectural constraints, or guarantees. Why different behavior on ResNet remains unexplained

strengths: Comprehensive empirical investigation with 150+ experiments across multiple architectures (GPT2, ResNet, MoE) and scales (124M-7B), including detailed ablations
Practical significance: claimed 5× speedup with minimal loss degradation has real value for large-scale model training
Insightful connection between initialization, muP scaling, and feature learning (Section 3.2), including the conflict between muP conditions and function-preserving initialization
Interesting empirical observation of 'mixing behaviors' where progressive training converges to fixed-size training under the right conditions
Transparent and actionable recipe (Section 7) with detailed hyperparameter reporting and extensive experimental ablations
weaknesses: Significant theory-practice gap: convex optimization analysis (Section 4) assumes non-convex deep learning dynamics; insights (e.g., smaller learning rates for t ≤ τ) are generic and don't mechanistically explain why WSD schedule specifically enables robust mixing across different expansion times

Critical dependency on design choices severely limits generalizability: WSD learning rate schedule is essential (cosine fails dramatically in Figure 5), Muon-NSGD optimizer outperforms AdamW (Figure 17), yet these are not novel. Method requires early-stopped runs to determine expansion timing, adding computational overhead

Questionable comparison fairness: authors acknowledge (Section 5.1) that mixing behaviors disappear with different measurement frames; the 5× speedup claim depends on comparing full pipeline (zero + expansion) vs. fixed target model, raising questions about whether advantage is inherent or frame-dependent

Incomplete understanding of core phenomenon: paper observes mixing behaviors empirically but provides no mechanistic explanation for why small-model features transfer to large models; model-dependent effects (random init less effective for ResNet, insertion ordering matters) suggest engineering complexity not fully addressed

Incremental novelty over concurrent work: progressive training is established; zero/one-layer expansion is straightforward pushdown; WSD schedule is known; unclear substantive differences from Du et al. (2024) who also explore shallow starting models. Main contributions are engineering optimizations, not conceptual advances

Initialization method lacks principled justification: random initialization works empirically but isn't theoretically motivated; produces large loss spikes (Figure 2) with unexplained recovery; model-dependent (works well on GPT2/MoE but less on ResNet)

Experimental limitations: heavy dependence on non-standard Muon-NSGD optimizer limits reproducibility and applicability; no head-to-head comparison with recent methods (Du et al. 2024, Pan et al. 2024) on identical benchmarks; MoE results limited to zero/one-layer only

Reproducibility concerns: expansion timing determination requires early-stopped runs; different models need different hyperparameter setups; reliance on recent/non-standard Muon-NSGD optimizer reduces accessibility

strengths: Strong empirical results: 5× speedup on GPT2 with <0.5% loss increase, substantially outperforming prior work (2-4×)
Comprehensive experimental validation: 150+ runs with systematic ablations across initialization strategies, timing, schedules, and optimizers; multiple architectures (GPT2, ResNet, MoE)

Novel conceptual contributions: characterizes 'mixing time' phenomenon and its robustness during WSD schedule; shows single-stage expansion suffices (contradicting prior multi-stage literature); interprets progressive training as 'PGD + initialization + SGD'

Rigorous feature learning analysis: connects to muP theory, clearly identifies conflict between function-preserving initialization and feature learning (Table 1), shows why zero initialization violates muP
Practical value: provides concrete recipe (Section 7), data-driven timing determination method, extensive reproducibility details in appendix
Honest presentation: transparently discusses how comparison perspectives affect results (Section 5.1); extensive ablations and negative results included; thorough limitations discussion
weaknesses: Theory-practice gap: convergence analysis assumes convex + Lipschitz loss but deep learning is non-convex; theory doesn't rigorously explain key empirical phenomena (e.g., robustness of mixing time to τ under WSD schedule)

Heavy dependence on WSD schedule: method requires specific warmup-stable-decay schedule; degrades with cosine schedule (0.8T expansion vs. 0.5T), which is more standard; limits generality and transferability

Perspective sensitivity (Section 5.1): mixing behaviors disappear when using standard (grown vs. target) comparison perspective, raising questions about robustness of core claims to different evaluation setups

Limited architectural diversity: primary evaluation on GPT2 and ResNet; MoE results are preliminary; no evaluation on modern architectures (modern transformers, other vision models); generalization unclear

muP/Muon-NSGD requirement: hyperparameter transfer requires muP-scaled optimizer with custom implementation; Figure 17 shows substantial performance gap with standard AdamW; claims about 'no hyperparameter tuning' overstated

Incomplete comparisons: limited direct head-to-head comparison with prior progressive training methods despite claiming 60× improvements; no wall-clock time comparisons accounting for communication overhead in distributed training

Narrow evaluation scope: only pre-training loss evaluated, no downstream task performance; single dataset per modality (OpenWebText, ImageNet); no interaction analysis with other efficiency techniques

Reproducibility limitations: no code release announced; custom optimizer implementation details in appendix; some hyperparameter choices (2% warmup, 10% decay, 80% expansion timing) lack explicit justification
Technical presentation: mixing time definition (L(·) ≈ L(·)) is informal; Figure 4 difficult to parse; architecture-dependent random initialization behavior (Section A.3) deserves deeper analysis
Limited theoretical applicability: convergence bounds derived for full training; practical early stopping regime not addressed; discrete-time theory vs. continuous optimization gap not discussed
